name: Teahupo'o
label: Teahupo'o
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Teahupo'o Wave Sign' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: World-famous surf break at the end of the road.

text.description: Teahupo'o is a small village on Tahiti's southeastern coast, home to roughly 1,500 people and served by a single one-lane road. It is known worldwide for the heavy surf that breaks off its shore. The wave is so hollow because it breaks over an extremely shallow coral reef, in places only about 51 cm (20 inches) below the surface. The village hosted the surfing at the 2024 Summer Olympics, which makes it a long way from Paris. For a phone photo, the most dependable picture is not of the wave itself. It is the village sign at the entrance, near Teahupo'o Beach, with the coastline and green hillsides behind it. Guides describe it as one of the most photographed spots in the village, and it makes a good arrival shot at the end of the road. Be realistic about the surf: from land the waves can look small, and the close-up wave pictures you see online are usually taken from a boat in the channel. If you want boats and surf in the frame, the landing at Debarcadère Teahupoo shows boats heading out through the channel, with the break and the mountains beyond the lagoon. Keep to the shore and never walk on the reef. Boat trips are paid, and they can be stopped on big-swell days, so ask locally.
text.geographic_location: Teahupo'o is a village on the southeastern coast of Tahiti, at the end of the coast road, with the lagoon and reef in front and steep green hills behind.
text.directions_text: No public transport is listed for this spot; check locally how to reach Teahupo'o. From wherever you are staying on Tahiti, head for the southeastern coast and the village of Teahupo'o. The sign is at the village entrance, near Teahupo'o Beach. The boat landing at Debarcadère Teahupoo is a second recommended viewpoint, so check locally how far it is from the sign. Parking at the landing may be charged, so check locally. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the sign with the coastline behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the hillsides in the frame. At the boat landing, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull in the boats and the surf beyond the lagoon.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand at the Teahupo'o Wave Sign, at the village entrance near Teahupo'o Beach. From here the sign sits in the foreground, with the coastline and lush hillsides behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the sign on one side, leaving the coast and hills to fill the rest of the frame. Crouch slightly so the sign stands out against the scenery. For a second picture, go to Debarcadère Teahupoo and frame the channel with a boat in the middle, using the mountain backdrop above it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sign to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the sign and hillsides keep their colour. Try a Live Photo at the landing to catch boats moving. Keep your phone strap or wrist loop on near the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Surf season runs roughly May to October, and the wave is best seen at high tide with offshore winds. If surf is your goal, plan around those conditions. For the sign photo, morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light.

text.access_note: The sign viewpoint is not listed as paid. Boat trips are paid, and parking at the landing may be charged, so check locally before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light for the sign photo.
Parking at the boat landing may be charged.
Crouching slightly helps the sign stand out against the scenery.

name: Mount Orohena
label: Mont Orohena
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mont Orohena' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).

text.description:
Mount Orohena is the highest point on Tahiti and in all of French Polynesia, at 2,241 metres (7,352 ft). It is an extinct shield volcano, and it ranks 7th in the world for topographic isolation. In plain terms, it stands well apart from any other high ground, which is why the view from the top reaches so far.

This is not a casual stop. The summit is a demanding two- to three-day trek, and hiking guides advise doing it with a guide. The reward is a 360-degree panorama over the interior valleys, the coast, Mo'orea and the Pacific, on a clear day. The usual place for photos is the summit outcrop, and it is worth the effort because you can turn on the spot and capture the whole island and the ocean around it.

For your phone, the big scenes are the point. Take a wide shot of the valleys, then a closer one of Mo'orea on the horizon. Cloud is the main risk, so be ready to wait a few minutes for a gap and keep your phone handy when it opens.

If the trek is not for you, Pointe Vénus on the northern coast shows Mount Orohena rising inland, framed by the bay and the lighthouse area. It is the easy, free option, but the mountain is often hidden by cloud, so check the sky before you go.
text.geographic_location: Mount Orohena stands in the high interior of Tahiti, the island's highest point.
text.directions_text: There is no public transport near the mountain. For the summit, arrange the trek with a local guide. The climb takes two to three days, so there is no short walking time to quote. For the easier view, Pointe Vénus on the northern coast is roadside-accessible and easy, but check the sky first. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of valleys and sea, then use the default lens (1x) for general shots. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Mo'orea and the coastline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Mont Orohena, at the summit outcrop. From here the photo shows a 360-degree panorama over the interior valleys, the coast, Mo'orea and the Pacific, on a clear day.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn slowly and take one wide shot in each direction rather than trying to fit everything in one frame. Use panorama mode for the sweep of the horizon. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level, and include a bit of the rock outcrop in the foreground to give a sense of height. For an alternative, Pointe Vénus shows the mountain rising inland across the bay.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the far land, then drag the exposure slider down a little so bright cloud and sea keep their detail. Take a few frames in case cloud moves across, and keep your phone battery topped up for the long trek.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when clouds are usually lower. One guide suggests May to September for clearer skies.

text.access_note: The summit is a demanding two- to three-day trek that is best done with a guide, so check the official site or a local guide operator before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Panorama mode works best with a slow, steady turn.
Phone batteries drain faster on a long trek, so carrying a power bank is sensible.

name: Point Venus
label: Point Venus
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plage de la Pointe Vénus' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plage de la Pointe Venus' (node/5536883221): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q25049114: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Black-sand headland with a historic lighthouse.

text.description: Point Venus is a palm-fringed headland on the north coast of Tahiti, at the north-eastern end of Matavai Bay. It is best known for its white-and-red lighthouse, which stands behind a beach of dark volcanic sand. For photographs, that dark sand, the green palms and the turquoise water behind or beside the lighthouse give you strong colour contrast in a single frame, and the lighthouse gives the picture a clear focal point. The headland also has real history. Captain James Cook anchored in Matavai Bay on 12 April 1769 to observe the Transit of Venus, and his party set up an observatory and a fortified camp here, which is how the place got its name. The lighthouse is no longer staffed but is looked after, and its open grounds are free to enter. The classic picture is taken from the beach in front of the lighthouse, looking straight at the tower, with palms framing the sides. Go early if you can: the cruise-ship day visitors arrive later, and the beach is quieter and the light softer in the morning. Golden hour is another popular time. For a second view, walk out along the headland and photograph back towards the lighthouse, with the beach and water in the frame. There is no marked spot for this, so look around when you arrive.
text.geographic_location: Point Venus is on the north coast of Tahiti, in the commune of Mahina, about 8 km east of Pape'ete. It sits at the north-eastern end of Matavai Bay.
text.directions_text: From Pape'ete, head about 8 km east along the north coast to Point Venus. Once on the headland, walk to the beach in front of the lighthouse. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view of the lighthouse with palms on either side. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the sand and sea, and keep the horizon level. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the tower from the beach or the headland.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (beach in front of the lighthouse, facing the tower). The white-and-red lighthouse framed by palms and black volcanic sand, with the turquoise water of Matavai Bay behind it. For an alternative, walk out along the headland (Pointe Vénus) and look back across to the lighthouse, with the beach and water in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the lighthouse on one of the vertical lines, with a palm or two in the foreground to frame it. Keep the dark sand in the lower third so it leads the eye to the tower. Crouch a little for a low angle that makes the lighthouse look taller. From the headland, include a curve of the beach so the lighthouse is not alone in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lighthouse to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the white tower keeps its detail and the sky and water stay rich in colour. If a shot looks too dark in the sand, nudge the slider back up. A Live Photo can catch the palms moving in the breeze.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the cruise-ship day visitors arrive; one guide suggests 6-7am. Golden hour is also recommended.

text.access_note: The beach and the lighthouse's open grounds are free to enter, but rules can change, so check locally before you go if you want to do anything beyond walking and photographing.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines, a low angle and the exposure slider will help with the white tower and dark sand (general phone-photography advice).
Palms moving in the breeze make a Live Photo worthwhile.

name: Marae Arahurahu
label: Marae Arahurahu
camera_source: Researched viewpoint ''Ārahurahu Marae' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W754462257 (Marae Arahurahu): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Restored ancient Polynesian temple in Paea.

text.description:
'Ārahurahu Marae is a restored sacred site set among greenery on Tahiti's west coast, in the Paea area. Stone platforms, a pathway and a courtyard make up the grounds. Two replica statues stand on the site: the female figure Moana, with her wide necklace, and a second figure, Heiata, a little further back.

For a phone photographer there are two good pictures here. The classic one is the restored stone pathway leading up through the courtyard to the altar platform, with the trees around it framing the stonework. The quieter one is a close, portrait-style photo of Moana, with Heiata softly visible behind her. If the pathway has other visitors on it, the statue pair is the easier shot to get clean.

The stone platforms are sacred and visitors may not walk on them, so take your photos from the paths and the edges of the grounds. Do not climb up for a better angle. Entry is reported as free, with parking nearby, but check the official site before you go in case that has changed.

Give yourself time to walk the whole site before choosing a spot. Keep your voice low and your pace slow, as this is a place of cultural importance and not just a backdrop.
text.geographic_location: On the west coast of Tahiti, in the Paea area (the Tefa'aiti valley).
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or bus stops are listed for this spot, so the easiest way is by taxi or hired scooter. Head for the Paea area on Tahiti's west coast and ask for 'Ārahurahu Marae. There is a car park at the site. Once inside, the phone icon on the map is beside the Moana statue, so follow the path to her. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the statue close-up, or the telephoto (2x or more) to squeeze Moana and Heiata closer together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long pathway shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you have a close view of her wide necklace, with the second statue, Heiata, standing behind her on the grounds.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Fill the frame with Moana and let Heiata sit softly in the background. Turn on the gridlines and place the necklace and face on one of the upper lines. For a different view, walk to the edge of the pathway and shoot along the restored stone path towards the altar platform, using the greenery as a frame. Stay off the platforms.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Try portrait mode for the statue so the background softens. Tap on Moana's face to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky behind is bright and the carving is turning dark or washed out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier or later in the day usually gives softer light on the carving and stonework. Under tree cover, a bright midday sun can leave harsh patches, so check each shot on the screen.

text.access_note: A sacred site where the stone platforms must not be walked on; entry is reported as free, but check the official site before you go for current access and any visiting etiquette.

name: Papeete Cathedral
label: Papeete Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place Notre Dame' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place Notre-Dame' (way/754789898): middle (108 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/32774088: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Papeete' (50 m across).
notes: Catholic cathedral in the centre of Papeete.

text.description:
Papeete Cathedral, dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, is the oldest Catholic church in Tahiti. It opened in 1875 and is one of the last examples of early colonial architecture left in Papeete. It stands close to the waterfront esplanade on the rue du Général de Gaulle, and its yellow front and red spire make it easy to pick out.

It photographs well because the entrance is a simple, strong shape: a yellow facade with a red steeple at the centre, which faces towards Mont Aorai. The open square in front gives you room to step back and fit the whole front into your frame. Some local address pages call the square Place de la Cathédrale, so check the name on the map.

From the square, start with the default lens (1x) and keep the spire in the middle of the frame. If you want to include the trees and planting around the building, walk to Parc Bougainville for a wider view. For a different angle with colourful buildings in the foreground, try Rue Colette. Early morning or late evening usually gives softer light and fewer people in your shot. Inside, the church is known for a woodcarving of the Madonna and Child from the Marquesas Islands, with the Child clutching a breadfruit, but check the rules on photography inside before you take your phone out.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Papeete, the capital of French Polynesia on the island of Tahiti, close to the waterfront esplanade on the rue du Général de Gaulle.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the waterfront esplanade in central Papeete. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are standing close and the front will not fit. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the red spire or the details of the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place Notre Dame (in front of the main facade). The yellow front of the cathedral with its red spire, framed by the open square in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the spire on the centre line so the front looks balanced. Hold the phone level and upright, and leave a little sky above the spire. For a different view, try Parc Bougainville, where the building sits among green trees and planting, or Rue Colette, where colourful buildings fill the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the yellow wall to set focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the red spire keeps its colour.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late evening, for softer light and fewer people in the square.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and any rules on photography or dress inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting the phone up to fit a tall spire can make the building lean, so keeping the phone level and upright helps.
Pulling the exposure slider down keeps a bright sky from washing out.
Visitors may be expected to dress modestly or may face limits on photography during services (not verified; hence the 'check the official site' advice).
The square in front of the cathedral is open to walk into without a ticket.

name: Papeete Market
label: Papeete Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Boulevard Pomare' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Boulevard de la Reine Pomare IV' (way/204588710): middle (38 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7132559: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Busy central market with flowers, crafts and pearls.

text.description: Papeete Market is the big municipal market in the middle of Papeete, the capital of Tahiti. Stalls sell fruit, vegetables, fish, oils, handicrafts such as hats and handbags, local textiles and souvenirs, including shell necklaces. That mix of produce and handmade goods is why it is such a good place to photograph. For a quieter shot of the exterior, walk to the waterfront stretch of Boulevard Pomare in front of the market doors. From the boulevard you can fit the market's harbour-side facade, the boulevard in the foreground and the island of Moorea in the background into one frame. Moorea is the main draw of this view and the facade is a secondary subject, so treat it as a setting shot rather than a close-up of the building. A guide recommends this stretch in the morning, when Moorea looks sharp across the water. It is also a calmer place to take pictures of the building once you have finished shopping inside. If you want a second picture, go up inside the building for a wide, high view over the produce, fish and flower stalls below. The market is busiest early in the morning, so expect crowds in the aisles at that time. Opening times can change, so check Tahiti Tourisme for the current times before you go. Take a few frames of the facade and a few of the stalls, so you have both the setting and the colourful goods.
text.geographic_location: The market is in central Papeete, the capital of Tahiti, on the waterfront side of town. Boulevard Pomare runs along the harbour in front of it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stops are listed for this spot. The Boulevard Pomare waterfront in front of the market doors is the viewing position for the facade and Moorea. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the facade, the boulevard and Moorea into one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the building. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to bring Moorea closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Boulevard Pomare (waterfront stretch directly in front of the market doors). The market's harbour-side facade with the waterfront boulevard in the foreground and Moorea on the horizon beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line, with the market on one side and the boulevard leading the eye along the bottom of the frame. Keep the phone level so the building does not lean. For a different picture, go inside and shoot from the upper floor for a wide overhead view of the produce, fish and flower stalls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the sea to set exposure, then use the exposure slider to bring down the brightness a little so the sky keeps its colour and Moorea stays visible. Tap the facade to focus. Indoors, tap on the stalls and use the default lens (1x) for sharper pictures in the shade.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when a guide notes that Moorea appears sharp on the horizon. The market itself is busiest early, so expect more people inside then.

text.access_note: The boulevard outside is a public street, but the market has opening times that may change, so check Tahiti Tourisme for the current times before you go.

name: Paul Gauguin Museum
label: Gauguin Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7150840: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Museum about the painter in a botanical garden.

text.description: The Paul Gauguin Museum is an art museum devoted to the life and work of the painter Paul Gauguin in Tahiti. It is built in a Japanese-influenced style, which makes the building itself a more interesting subject than many small museums. It stands at PK 51 in Papeari, directly across from the Botanical Gardens, so the green setting helps your photos. Inside, the exhibits cover French Polynesian and Marquesan culture, with original Gauguin documents, photographs, reproductions, sculptures, engravings and gouaches. The museum closed in 2013 for renovation, and a sister museum in Hiva Oa is open. Please check the current situation before planning a visit around it. For a phone photo, the aim is a simple record of the building with its garden surroundings. Stand back far enough to include the roofline and some of the greenery, keep the phone level so the straight lines of the architecture stay straight, and leave a little space around the edges. If the doors or grounds are closed, you can still take good photos of the exterior from wherever public access allows. Take one wide shot to show the setting, then move closer for a detail of the façade, a doorway or the planting. Photograph signs or entrance details too, as they help you remember the place later.
text.geographic_location: In the Papeari district of Tahiti, at PK 51, directly across from the Botanical Gardens.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stops are listed for this place. The museum is at PK 51 in Papeari, directly across from the Botanical Gardens, so look for the gardens as a landmark. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building and its garden setting. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you have to stand close, but keep the building centred to avoid stretched edges. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for façade details and roof lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there the building is right in front of you, so stand back to fit in the whole frontage with some greenery around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the roof and walls with them so the building looks straight. Include some of the surrounding plants for a sense of place, and take a second, closer shot of one architectural detail. Respect any signs or barriers while you are framing.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the bright sky is washing out the walls. Do not use portrait mode on the building; keep it for people in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the walls. An overcast day also works well for even colour in the greenery.

text.access_note: The museum has been closed for renovation, so check the official site before you go to see whether it is open and what access is allowed.
